She promptly accepted such a condition: «From now on the thought of your bride will be nothing other than to suffer» 40.

The feast of the Sacred Heart is every year an occasion of extraordinary graces. She mentions the Heart of the Redeemer very often in her diary and letters. In 1873 it happened that she celebrated this feast during a journey on which she had some cruel sufferings. She went to a church where there was an image of the Sacred Heart to thank Him and offer Him that suffering. «As soon as I looked at Him — she writes — He smiled at me. My Good, are you pleased with my suffering and my acting? How glad I am!» (M 4.1, p. 107).

It is not the only time that the smiling countenance of Jesus reassures her of his pleasure. At other times, however, she finds his face sad, which she interprets as a sign of some wrong committed perhaps unawares (cf. M 4.2, p. 54f). On 10 February 1876, feeling exhausted in strength, she prayed the Lord to come to her aid so that no one would notice her weakness; wholly absorbed in ecstasy, she saw a stream come out of the Heart of Jesus that poured into her mouth and nourished her. When the vision ended, she felt strong and robust (M 4.4, p. 31). One night in the month of March of the same year she had a new vision: «a most beautiful Heart, all aflame, with a white circle around it», wrapped in great splendor; it left her flooded with immense sweetness and enlightened with new teachings (M 4.4, p. 395). Another similar favor she received in the month of December 1877:

«My Good gave me such sweetness in opening his Side to me! It seemed that into this his Heart there poured that sweetest honey of his love… Ah! Love! why do you pour so many graces into so perverse a creature?… I have no more tastes, I have no more pleasures: only you! And for you I live, for you and in you I will die» (M 4.5, p. 215).

40 Considerations on the heart that receives the essence of the love of Jesus. Writings of Mother Rosa, Bundle 62, no. 4.

p. 1011

And here is yet another of her outpourings of love, addressed in the month of September 1880:

«Oh! sweetest Heart, source of all my relief! Yes, in you alone my soul, oppressed by the toils of sufferings, finds in you refreshment and life; in you I find my living and all my pains in you grow sweet, Vesuvius of love! for whoever rests upon you sleeps no other sleep than of love. In you alone, yes, I experience the all; from this Vesuvius spring forth every kind of treasures. Oh! how blind is man! he does not know where the true good lies» (M 5.1, p. 285).

Her mother's heart, when she writes to the daughters of St. Anne, finds no more fitting way to express her affection to them than to meet each one in the Heart of Jesus. It would be endless to wish to gather the warm expressions in which she affirms simultaneously her love for the Lord and for the addressee.

Every day she made as it were an oblation to the eternal Father, in the mercy-seat of the Heart of Jesus, of her Institute, not as of an organized and operating structure, but as of a living reality, made up of individual persons, each with her vocation, with her effort of sanctification, with her responsibilities, with her problems. It was her prayer as foundress:

«My God! to you I entrust these creatures whom you have entrusted to me. Now I place them for all this time in the Heart of your Son Jesus, and may you cover them with heavenly dew, that they may be defended from every slightest encounter. In this loving retreat of the Heart of Jesus may they learn the true school of your divine Love. My God, bless them and strengthen them in suffering, pour upon them the choicest blessings» (L to Sr. A. Paola Bucciotti: 25-5-1871).

3. The Eucharist, the mystery of love

From youth Rosa distinguished herself by her Eucharistic piety. In the first years of widowhood she spent long hours before the Sacrament. And it was precisely while she was in adoration, in 1859, that she had the first vision of the Lord (M 1.1, p. 2). The Eucharistic mystery will become for her something vital, whether as nourishment of the spirit in the Sacrament, as bond of oblation in the Sacrifice, or as attraction of love in the Tabernacle. Communion, life of the soul

From 1855, authorized by her confessor, she enjoyed the benefit of daily communion, uncommon in that time (FIOCCHI, I, p. 53). And already from then she was favored with the mystical gift of sensible taste in holding the holy Host in her mouth, with an «indescribable consolation» (M 1.1, p. 18, 30).

For nothing in the world would she have given up communion. On journeys she made great sacrifices to be able to receive it; one must take into account the rigid discipline of the Eucharistic fast then in force; sometimes she fasted for three days, eating nothing from one communion to the next, faithful to her rule of not eating fat (M 4.5, p. 56; cf. Summ., p. 579). We can understand what her sorrow was on that terrible 31 March 1869 when the superior, Fr. Tornatore, deprived her of holy communion, after 14 and a half years in which she had never missed it (M 1.2, p. 23).

Communion was the privileged moment of her mystical ascents. She remained in thanksgiving for about an hour, kneeling on the floor and leaning with one arm on a chair, motionless and insensible to everything external. To those who asked what she said in such long hours, she answered: «Before Jesus time has no time» (FIOCCHI, II, p. 358). Very often the interior absorption was so intense that, to avoid being rapt, she had to plead: «O Love! please! for pity's sake, I am in church, I fear they will notice; wait until I am in my room. Withdraw, for pity's sake!» (M 1.1, p. 1275).

In order to prolong during the day and the night the effects of sacramental communion she made frequent spiritual communions, especially on journeys each time she caught sight of the bell tower of a church; and very often she experienced the effects of the sacrament, as if she really received it (M 4.4, p. 106; 4.5, p. 118).

She encouraged the sisters to feed with fervor on the Eucharistic bread and then to live the day giving themselves to work with the strength of this nourishment. In a circular of 23 April 1893 she recommended that all give such importance to holy communion that it might «bind together all the actions of the day». United to the sacrifice of the altar

She had become accustomed to associating herself with Jesus, Priest and Victim, in the sacrifice of the Mass; but one day she received special light on the universality of the one Sacrifice, which is offered constantly in all latitudes of the world, and she took up devotion to this practice:

«While I was hearing Mass and offering to the eternal Father the Sacrifice of the altar, a most vivid light appeared to me, together with a voice that said to me:

— This sacrifice of yourself in that chalice, together with his beloved Son, pleases God greatly; but it would please Him greatly if you offered yourself as victim in all the Sacrifices that are performed on the altars of the whole Catholic world.

And at once I do not delay in doing it. As soon as I had done this, I remained absorbed in God, and my intellect clearly saw all the Sacrifices performed and yet to be performed in all the Catholic churches. I rejoiced greatly; and so every morning I renew the offering: Behold, my God, your victim who unites herself to Jesus, your Son, to be immolated upon the altar. in the bloody chalice, which offers itself to you as Victim of expiation for sinners» (M 1.1, p. 1235).

Some years later she describes a similar offering, «very pleasing to the eternal Father» (M 1.1, p. 179).

The treasure of the Eucharistic presence

The «great mystery of our faith» had become the continual object of her adoration and her love. She remained absorbed before this «unique and immense treasure of our soul» (L to Emilia di Fitalia: 4-9-1889). Very often this faith was transformed into experience through vision, especially when in adoration with the Blessed Sacrament exposed; but also when she contemplated it enclosed in the tabernacle. She prayed thus one day in 1866:

«Satisfy me, for pity's sake, with your love! Oh! why do I not remain forever before your ciborium where, my Beloved, you are enclosed? What are five, six hours a day? A nothing! Let me remain close to you without moving any more… Light of my eyes, sweet Love of mine! If men knew you, surely they would leave everything and come to the feet of your altar to enjoy your delights. But how can I make them understand?…» (M 1.1, p. 435).

She was happy when, on her visit to Pius IX, in January 1866, she obtained from the Pontiff an autograph by which he granted her the faculty of keeping the Blessed Sacrament in the house (FIOCCHI, I, p. 109). At Piacenza she wished to have her little cell adjoining the chapel; thus, even during the night, she directed to Jesus in the sacrament her acts of adoration and her affections through the little window opened in the wall. She often speaks of the long stretches of time she spent absorbed in close union with Him, sometimes even the whole night (M 3, p. 79; 4.1, pp. 125, 18; 4.4, pp. 265, 95f, 1148).

One of the forms of her piety, always original, was that of moving in spirit to the chapels of the various houses of the Institute to unite herself with her spiritual daughters in the homage of love to the Lord present in the tabernacle (M 4.1, p. 87f). She taught them to have recourse to Him in difficult moments:

«If you find yourself sad, run to church and cry out, weep with Jesus, and then, once you have dried your tears, back to work again, all things to all and full of sweet unction to produce it in others» (L to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 13-5-1872).

Eucharistic adoration, although not prescribed by the Rule, became habitual in the houses of the Daughters of St. Anne with a sufficient number of sisters, above all in the Mother House. But because of their mission in service of the Church they could not give themselves full time to such an act of worship; so Mother Rosa welcomed with joy the offer by the bishop of Piacenza, Mgr. Scalabrini, of the direction of an institute for deaf-mute girls opened by him in 1880. The interest she felt for those creatures, being the mother of a deaf-mute daughter, came to be joined to her desire to see Jesus adored in the Eucharist. On 8 December 1884, with the clothing of the first five deaf-mutes, the community of the Tertiaries of St. Anne, Perpetual Adorers of the Most Blessed Sacrament, began 41.

4. Holy mother Church

Rosa Gattorno's profound sense of Church would deserve a separate treatise. It is not only submission to the representatives

41 Cf. FIOCCHI, I, pp. 166-171; II, p. 53. The biographer's version of the origin of the community of the Adorers is different, but it does not seem documentarily reliable. of the hierarchical Church, but a true ecclesial spirituality inspired by faith and nourished by veneration and love. Raised in a family environment where she had to deal with Freemasons and anticlericals, she had to mature from youth her fidelity to mother Church, a fidelity that became service and apostolic industry, seeking from the beginning to make sure of the authenticity of her initiatives through the approval and guidance of the diocesan authority.

It was obedience to the archbishop of Genoa Mgr. Charvaz that made her accept, in 1864, at the insistent request of the Servant of God Fr. Giuseppe Frassinetti, first the presidency of the Daughters of Mary and then the charge of superior of the nascent Pious Union of the Daughters of Mary Immaculate, the new Ursulines. And it was the same archbishop who verified the genuineness of the divine impulse that drove her to found a new institute and encouraged her to go personally to Pope Pius IX to make sure, from the lips of the supreme Pastor, that this was God's will.

As foundress, she was intimately convinced that the institute of the Daughters of St. Anne was not only a Work of God, but was born in the Church and for the Church. Mother Rosa made her own the ideas of Fr. Tornatore, who wrote in a circular letter of 1876:

«The heavenly Father, who is the one who planted our poor Institute in the garden of his Church, looks upon it with an eye of special predilection. He increased its houses and multiplied its members… and, with the increase of the sisters, has been pleased to establish it ever more firmly in the spirit of its vocation».

As a true daughter of the Church, she experienced as her own the vicissitudes of the Bride of Christ; indeed, she saw in the internal sufferings of her Institute an almost repercussion of the common tribulations of the people of God. Thus she expressed it in a letter in the disquieting days of the usurpation of the Papal States:

«It is a time of work and of much suffering in this work of the Lord: the Church is afflicted and so everything that belongs to her suffers torment and pain» (L to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 28-12-1870).

But there was also a repercussion of a mystical nature, which she describes in her Memoirs. Sometimes the suffering touches the very support of her faith, in an atrocious passive purification:

p. 1016

«I am in the greatest desolation: horrible temptations against the Church. And who am I? My God, I am a monster of infamy! when for the Pope and the Princes Cardinals, the Bishops, what would I not do? My life is nothing to offer for the prosperity of the holy Church. Alas! how painful this state is to me!» (M 5.2, p. 46, 1884).

On Good Friday 1885 she had an experiential participation in the sorrows of the Lord's Passion. Amid turmoil and agonies, the spasms of the dislocation of the bones, in the crucifixion, she felt identified with the sufferings of the Church, the mystical Body of Christ in which the Passion is always renewed:

«What I have suffered, my God! First there came upon me something I do not know how to describe, and I said: O my Love! what is this that I feel? — They are the pains that the Church suffers!» (M 5.3, p. 745).

The book Labors and Consolations ends with a beautiful allegory of the suffering Church: seven tablets reddened with blood, supported by bands of fire; St. Peter weeping, while a legion of angels sadly sings; the faithful souls dressed in mourning, in the midst of a mass of indifferent men. «From time to time a loud groan came forth from them…: it was heartrending…: it is the Church that suffers!». Rosa offers herself as victim to repair the cause of such sadness and to console mother Church (TC, p. 3808).

She prayed and had others pray for the Church. She offered her permanent fast, as well as the pain of the invisible stigmata, «for holy Mother Church, for the supreme Pontiff, for the Cardinals and the Bishops» (M 1.1, pp. 135, 161).

She, however, does not belong to the number of those prophets of misfortune who see everything black in the life of the Church and in its future. In the month of February 1878 she had a vision on the state of things at that historical moment, and understood that «the abyss, in which the world now stands, will change in an instant, with the fair triumph of the Church coming» (M 4.5, p. 31).

This ecclesial faith of hers is centered above all on the Roman Pontiff. Toward Pius IX she nourished not only sentiments of obedience and veneration, but of true devotion, since at the feet of this Pope she felt confirmed, as has been said, in her charism as foundress and encouraged to leave to God the care of her children. In her writings she calls him «this holy Pope», «the great saint» (M 2, pp. 66, 69). After the occupation of Rome she thought of the Pontiff's situation: «The head of the Church imprisoned, Pius IX, my Father: oh! what torment!» (M 1.2, p. 29).

On 9 January 1876 she was again received in audience by Pius IX, and then communicated, full of emotion, to the sisters the words of affection and encouragement of the holy Father (LCirc 1876). The following year, in another circular, signed by her together with Fr. Tornatore, she expressed herself in these terms:

«He (Pius IX) nourishes a singular affection for our Institute, because our Institute was raised up by the Lord in his Church so that it might honor in an altogether special way that venerable Matron in whose womb was wrought the mystery of the Immaculate Conception of Mary, from the definition of which mystery the holy Father Pius IX draws that so great glory, by which he shines above all the Popes, as the sun shines more than the stars. This is why our Institute, in these its beginnings, has founded the greatest number of houses and goes on founding them in the Pope's State and, so to speak, around his Throne, because between the holy Father Pope Pius IX and our Institute there is a secret sympathy…» (L Circ. 1877).

It is easy to understand the sorrow experienced by Mother Rosa on 7 February 1878 when, being at Spello, she had the sign of the death of her beloved Pius IX (M 4.5, p. 235; Summ., p. 436). From that date she will commend herself, and will have the sisters commend themselves, to the intercession of the holy Pope in the needs of the Institute.

Enthusiasm for the popular as well as controversial Pius IX did not prevent her from professing the same dedication to his successor Leo XIII, as she manifested in the circular of 1 January 1879.

Let it not be forgotten, however, that if personal relations with the diocesan bishops and with the supreme Pontiffs Pius IX and Leo XIII were easy and full of consolation, the same cannot be said of dealings with the Roman dicasteries concerning the insertion of the Institute into the structural frameworks of the Church. The foundress had to suffer setbacks, misunderstandings, even harsh humiliations, which more than once put to a severe test her unshakable trust in the hierarchical Church. Here is how she expresses it, in her metaphorical language:

p. 1018

«Having tied the boat up well, as best I knew how, I sought to make my way to my Good in his great temple, to his Vicar. Oh! what a surprise! Thus ill-clad, beggarly as I was, a poor slave of the Lord, I kissed the foot and the hand of his Vicar. O most humble sovereign! O mercy of God! The Vicar asks me about the little ship, wishes it near him and prophesies the future to me. O my Savior! with what breath I had run to take the little vessel to bring it where the Vicar wanted! But a stormy sea rises, a contrary wind rages and dashes me upon a rock… After a little struggle my little ship came out more beautiful… Brought to the feet of Peter, I knew not what else to say to him except that he should say many things for me to my God: that I was bringing the little vessel to the feet of his Vicar, that it might be incorporated into his Church» (TC, pp. 218-220).

The first great trial was the order received, in February 1872, from the Holy Office, through the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars and Cardinal Vannicelli, Protector of the Institute, to withdraw and burn all copies of the Rules and to remove the co-founder Fr. Tornatore. Mother Rosa obeyed without delay; she stayed up all night to send to all the houses the order imposed; the next day she wrote to the Cardinal's secretary:

«God's will be done upon our superiors; and I, miserable creature, with my head to the ground, adore all his dispositions and submit myself to the wishes of the Church» (Fiocchi, I, p. 232; Summ., pp. 238-239).

Another delicate moment was the situation created, in 1881, after the general chapter's refusal of the amendments proposed by the Holy See, the most important of which was the constitution of a general council. The foundress bore, with God's help, the harsh reproof of the Cardinal Prefect of the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars. In a humble letter she acknowledged the fault unintentionally committed and what the chapter had done was retracted. Everything ended with a letter from the same Cardinal praising the full submission of the superior general and her council to the dispositions of the Holy See 42.

Mother Rosa felt compensated for so many bitternesses in the audience granted her by Leo XIII in April 1885: the Pope questioned her

42 FIOCCHI, II, pp. 37-42; R. FRATI, The Chapter of 1888, in Virga Jesse, n. s. 4 (1988) no. 2. at length about the Institute and showed himself very pleased with what the Daughters of St. Anne were doing. Comforted with the papal blessing, she came out of that audience «drunk with consolation» (FIOCCHI, II, p. 575).

The third and last great trial, which came to refine still further her fidelity to the hierarchical Church, was the apostolic visitation of the Institute, begun on 28 July 1898 by the Benedictine abbot Dom Domenico Serafini by order of the Cardinal Prefect of the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars; it had been motivated by certain unfounded accusations about some administrative irregularities and by the printing of the volume Labors and Consolations, which had been denounced to the Holy Office. When the visitor presented his credentials to her and told her the object of the measure, Mother Rosa could not master her emotion; she said through tears: «I already know that I am good for nothing, that I ruin everything: therefore I resign from this moment…». Then, encouraged by Dom Serafini himself, she recovered and collaborated with him with all sincerity (FIOCCHI, II, pp. 179-188; Summ., p. 256). A month later, on 30 August 1898, thanking the community of Piacenza for the homage on the occasion of her name day, she gave a most beautiful address to the sisters and said, with clear allusion to the trial she was going through:

«Yes, love the Mother, love her in the holy Church… Little daughters, one promise I want from you on this day: that you be faithful to the Institute and to holy Mother Church. No, little daughters, let not calumnies, anxieties, anguish make you fail in the holy vocation… I too was calumniated, despised, mistreated: and not even the slightest thought against the holy vocation came to me…» (Fiocchi, II, p. 2775).

Death reached the foundress while the apostolic visitation was still in progress. The visitor himself, having become Cardinal, was invited to testify in the informative process of Rome and made a sincere eulogy of the Institute, which he knew well.

The same attitude of obedience and veneration she observed and wanted observed toward the prelates of the dioceses where the Institute had houses. When it was necessary, for the approval of the Constitutions, it was not difficult for her to gather laudatory letters of recommendation from numerous bishops, satisfied with the life and services of the Daughters of St. Anne. She sent, by letter, a strong reproof to a mistress of novices because she did not teach the young women to show outwardly reverence toward the ministers of God (L to Sr. A. Francesca Savignoni: 23-3-1880). She could not bear that anyone speak ill of them. «Jesus is jealous of his ministers»; He has reserved to Himself the right to judge them (cf. L to Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi: undated; to Emilia di Fitalia: 21-6-1893). On 18 March 1874 she left written a page of great affliction, being unable to quiet her spirit after having spoken unfavorably of a priest, in secret, «to someone who could remedy certain scandals». She made acts of repentance and humiliation, «tightly pressed to mother Church» (M 4.2, pp. 57-61).

She recommended to the sisters to help the parish priests in catechetical instruction and in other pastoral needs, but without any compensation (Summ., p. 350).

Cardinal Granito di Belmonte, who was an immediate witness of Mother Rosa's reactions in the face of the sufferings she had to bear, testified in the informative process:

«In all the time of her life, on the many occasions when ecclesiastics were to her and her Institute a cause of displeasure and of very great adversity, the Servant of God had as her maxim never to let others know what might give occasion to lessen the reputation of those same ecclesiastics» (Summ., p. 10).

5. The Virgin Mary, sweetest Mother

Marian piety, tender and filial, occupies in Rosa Gattorno's religiousness its place, so to speak, theologically right, indeed almost a second plane, in comparison with the reality of God and the centrality of the Redeemer.

Already before being foundress she recited the Office of Our Lady (M 1.1, p. 11). She invoked her as Mother, as Advocate, as Teacher…; she had recourse to her in difficulties and in battles (M 1.1, p. 19). Mary entered fully into her unitive experiences when she contemplated the Passion of the Lord (M 1.1, p. 36), as also when she rejoiced in the triumph of the Resurrection. On the feast of Easter 1863 she addressed to Mary this fervent prayer:

p. 1021

«Come! Mary, most beloved Mother, remember this poor creature, who is down here immersed in darkness, because so little do you keep me with you and then to this miserable earth I return… O Mary! for the joy you feel today, release from her chains this poor creature…, and give me only Love. May my living be forever to suffer and to bear pain for Jesus… Come! become my Teacher and teach me what I must do to make myself less displeasing to my dear Jesus and to satisfy the many debts contracted by my failings…» (M 1.1, p. 38f).

On the eves of Marian feasts she was accustomed to spend the night «in contemplation always with Mary» (M 1.1, p. 81), often favored with visions that left her greatly consoled. She writes in 1876:

«The night I spent together with my dear Mother Mary. She stayed near me all night; she comforted me, and I felt something descend into me of peace, resignation and strength to be able the next day to resume work. Now she exhorted me and gave me most beautiful lessons, now she assured me that what I suffered was very dear to Jesus and that He was with me in it. Oh sweetest Mama!… The next day, full of vigor, nothing could cast me down… Oh Mary, my sweetness! you are always my comfort in the atrocious pains in which I find myself» (M 1.1, pp. 92f, 96).

One day in the month of May, after having experienced, throwing herself at Mary's feet in a moment of «despair», her presence as «a balsamic dew», she poured out her heart in expressions like these:

«O Mary! through you I am saved, through you I am a religious! The fire of your Son's love, Mary! with your hands more than once you kindled it in this heart of your Son. Oh! already, Love, why do you not make me die of this?…» (M 4.4, p. 565).

From time to time such outpourings of love to Our Lady spring from her inflamed heart:

«Mary, sweetest and dearest Mother: yours I was and am! Come! press me to Jesus that I may die of Him!» (M 4.4, p. 108) — «Mary, Mary! my life you are! Ask your servant, who will always, always obey you» (M 4.5, p. 195) «My life, after my God» (M 5.3, p. 29) — «Mary, Mary most holy, Mother of my Love» (TC, p. 30).

In her letters to the religious she recommends that they place everything in Mary's hands, as she herself does; or remember that the Sorrowful Mother suffered in her heart pains more atrocious than any a religious can meet.

She ended almost all her journeys with a visit to some shrine of Our Lady. In her last years she made four visits to the Holy House of Loreto, and there she remained for hours, motionless in prayer, as if in ecstasy (Summ., p. 260-261).

The first title given to the projected Institute, at Genoa, was Daughters of the Immaculate. When at Piacenza that of «Daughters of St. Anne» was adopted, the foundress wanted the relation to the Immaculate to remain, even in the name, a relation likewise desired by Fr. Tornatore.

The church of the generalate house, in Rome, was dedicated, by the will of the foundress herself, to Mary Mother of grace and mercy. It was the invocation of the «Madonnina», a small image, which the Venerable Fr. Bernardo Maria Clausi had always carried with him, and which then passed into the hands of Fr. Tornatore. Mother Rosa made it the object of her particular devotion, placed it in the chapel of the mother house of Piacenza and, in gratitude for the healing obtained on 29 April 1883 and for the help received for the construction of the house in Rome, wanted it to be crowned by Bishop Mgr. Scalabrini. When the church of Via Merulana was consecrated, the image was transferred to it 43.

6. St. Anne, the Mother of the Institute

The fact of entrusting the direction of the nascent Institute to Fr. Tornatore entailed for the foundress a costly sacrifice: having to change the name, adopting that of Daughters of St. Anne. «In no way could I adapt myself to loving her and having her as mother», she sincerely states, notwithstanding the vision she had of the Immaculate and of St. Anne (M 2, p. 57). But soon she let herself be convinced by the fervor of the co-founder for the Mother of the Mother of God.

In reality it was the beginning of a form of spirituality with which she fully identified herself in her task as foundress. She wished to take the habit on the feast of St. Anne, 26 July 1867, and to assume the name Anne,

43 Cf. R. FRATI, Maria Mater Gratiae et Misericordiae. Significato di una presenza, in Virga Jesse, n. s. 2 (1986) no. 2, pp. 12-22. placing it before that of baptism, an example that has been followed by all the Daughters of St. Anne.

It can be said that, more than a devotion centered on the Saint as such, it is an aspect of Marian piety: for Mother Rosa, St. Anne is worthy of veneration and enjoys a particular power of intercession, because in her womb the immaculate conception of the Mother of God was accomplished; hence the full title of the Institute was written by her and by Fr. Tornatore in this form: Daughters of St. Anne, Mother of the Immaculate. The Mother of Mary thus becomes the model of each of her daughters for her docility to God's plan, for her solicitude in nourishing and caring for the Child Mary even amid maternal sufferings and worries. Thus it was expressed in one of the leaflets intended to make the Institute known:

«The proper purpose, which distinguishes the Daughters of St. Anne…, is to make profession of giving a quite special worship to the glorious St. Anne, Mother of the Immaculate… The Institute (professes) also, among other virtues, the compassion of the heart of St. Anne, giving assistance to the sick at home… Thus they take in poor girls in danger, to preserve them from losing innocence and virtue: and here too they honor the care that (St. Anne) had of the Immaculate Child and the zeal that the Saint will have had through this care to see all the young girls of the world innocent» 44.

In her Memoirs she not only attributes a supernatural origin to the title of the Institute, but recognizes as an infused gift the love she began to profess to the Saint after her apparitions at Piacenza:

«Beautiful was the holy Mother in the act of caressing me. She came very close and communicated to me a love for her, so strong, that I must confess that in no way could I adapt myself to loving her and having her as Mother… The love for St. Anne had penetrated so strongly into me, that all the reluctance I had vanished, and it grew strong to such a point, that in all my needs I invoked her and always found myself satisfied: in providence, in journeys, in everything…» (M 2, p. 575).

She feels supported, guided, enlightened by the holy Mother in every concern; she is convinced that the progress of God's Work is owed

44 Arch. FSA, IcM - 9, pos. B. 1.61. The original sheet is in Fr. Tornatore's own hand. to the assistance of such a teacher. But she also experiences in her habitual closeness to her almost a mirror that helps her discern when things are going well and when not:

«My star, St. Anne, every morning marks the day for me, because, if I must go through tribulations, she lets herself be seen pale and sad, if deaths or things that the sisters do that are not right and that are against the holy Rule, she is covered with a black veil…» (M 4.5, p. 1435).

She acknowledged St. Anne as the first superior of the Institute; as a sign of this she tied the key of the Piacenza house to a statuette of the holy Mother (Summ., p. 430). In the annual circulars she ardently inculcates in the sisters devotion and love toward the Saint, proposes her as model of a true religious, insists on the efficacy of her protection on the Institute's path: «She rules it, defends it, governs it» (LCirc: 1876, 17-7-1899). She wants her to be invoked in every community, her image to preside not only over every chapel of the Institute, but also over every activity of the sisters; and that they strive to spread her devotion among the faithful.

The communal expression, which the Daughters of St. Anne repeat very often, is the ejaculation Blessed be, etc. We read in the circular of 1877:

«In this ejaculation there is contained a profession of faith, by which we believe that Mary, in the womb of our holy Mother, at the first instant of her conception was conceived there Immaculate… And since this ejaculation is almost continual from morning to night, so with it the Institute makes as it were continually the act of faith in the immaculate conception of Mary».

Mother Rosa, however, did not fail to warn the sisters against the danger of an inconsistent devotionalism. St. Anne is not the term of true piety: the same maternal task she had in her life, of giving Mary to the world and, through Mary, giving Jesus to the world, she exercises also now; if she attracts the affection of her daughters it is to make grow in them the love of Mary and of Jesus (cf. LCirc 1887).

«How many facts I could mention to show you how the holy Mother, Mother of the great Mother of God, wants to be invoked by her daughters in their needs and loved as Mother who to the great most holy Virgin and to blessed God leads us! She loves us, so that in these two hearts of Jesus and Mary you may all be purified, consumed in this sweetest love» (L Circ. 27-5-1892).

Indeed, I would dare say that, with the passing of the years, one observes in the foundress's writings almost a need to ground genuinely the concepts on the role of St. Anne in the spirituality of the Institute, to find a more theological climate.

Someone might judge strange and without biblical support a spirituality inspired by St. Anne mother of the Immaculate, but devotion to this great Saint is fully grounded in the worship that the Church has been paying for centuries to the Mother of the Mother of God, especially in the East, where a liturgy and an iconography of great expressive value have developed 45.

The Special Chapter of the Daughters of St. Anne carried out a deepening on the biblical basis of the Institute's spirituality: St. Joachim and St. Anne are seen in the line of the anawim who awaited the Lord, among whom «Mary, Mother of the Lord, stands out» (cf. Spiritualità di Avvento, pp. 15-19).

7. St. Francis of Assisi, «our Father»

Rosa Gattorno knew how to join to her eminently contemplative life a concrete and creative piety, which she transmitted to her religious. She dedicated the month of January to the eternal Father, March to St. Joseph, May to the Virgin Mary, June to the Sacred Heart of Jesus, July to St. Anne.

Her devotion to St. Joseph was linked to her faith in divine Providence; she called him «my dear protector». St. Michael the Archangel was invoked by her as her defender in dangers, in a special way in the struggle against demons, and as guide on journeys.

But the saint to whom she felt closest, after St. Anne, was St. Francis of Assisi. In the church of the generalate house in Rome she wished to dedicate an altar to each of the Institute's protectors: St. Anne, St. Francis of Assisi, St. Francis of Paola and St. Michael.

There is a relation between her longing to arrive at full trans-

In 1858, as a sign of the new life begun, she took the cord of St. Francis. In 1861 she donned the Franciscan habit, «like that of the friars, of the same cloth, obtained from the same». She wore it day and night under her usual clothes, with great sacrifice (M 1.1, pp. 1f, 8).

The seraphic Father became from then on stimulus and model of her gift of herself to Love by the way of total stripping. She prayed in these terms:

«My Love, consume me! It is all yours, O my Love! it is true, because if there were anything that did not please you and were not yours, oh! tell me, for at once I will say like my Father St. Francis: that if he had anything that was not God's, he would at once remove it. O my Love! and I would burn it!» (M 1.1, p. 11) 46.

On 24 September 1861, being on holiday at S. Francesco d'Albaro, she made profession in the Third Order of St. Francis. «And this good Father — she notes — I chose as my advocate and protector of my soul» (M 1.1, p. 13).

She would have wished, at the beginning, to insert her Institute into the great Franciscan family, with the title of «Daughters of Mary Immaculate, Minims of St. Francis of Assisi». And although, as we have seen, she consented to the will of the co-founder to place it under the protection and guidance of St. Anne, she did not wish thereby to discard St. Francis either from her personal spirituality or from the commitment of God's Work. In the vision she had on that occasion her seraphic Father had appeared to her together with Mary Immaculate and St. Anne (M 2, p. 58). One of her favorite ejaculations was that well known one of the Saint of Assisi: «My Good, my All» (M 4.1, p. 102). Every year she celebrated with fervor his feast (4 October) and that of his Stigmata (17 September), receiving in them great consolations (cf. M 1.2, p. 79; 5.1, p. 218; 11.1, p. 23). In 1880 she wished to prepare herself for the

The next day she had such a fire of love that she was forced to withdraw to her little room:

«O Love! I took my Crucified in my arms and, as usual, laid my head on his side, and there, what did I feel? You, my dear seraphic Father St. Francis, could say it, your tongue could explain it, but I cannot!» (M 5.1, p. 24).

She dedicated to St. Francis the Wednesday fast. She invoked his help very often. In her little room at Piacenza she always had an oleograph of the Saint, which was very dear to her. To encourage her religious to accept difficulties and sufferings, she recalled to them the already cited couplet of the seraphic Father: «So great is the good I await — that every pain is a delight to me». In a letter to Fr. Gennaro Granito di Belmonte she sought to justify her little care of her body in illnesses with the example of her model: «St. Francis, what did he make of his body? I have done nothing else than seek to imitate him as much as I could» (L 12-1-1889).

In 1871 she had a strange foretelling of her death, at the moment of which she wanted to have the consolation of seeing herself a daughter of St. Francis: «My Love came to console me. He made me see what will happen at my death…: the tertiary habit will be my habit, and the rest St. Anne's» (M 1.1, p. 164).

She always felt bound to the sons of St. Francis. In her Genoa years she associated familiarly with the popular Capuchin lay brother St. Francis of Camporosso († 1866), who is said to have predicted to her how much she would have to suffer to arrive at her success as foundress (Summ., p. 235); she nourished toward him a true veneration; in the Memoirs she calls him «my Brother Francis»; she had some apparitions of him (M 4.1, p. 5).

In Naples she met a Brother Angelo, a Franciscan lay brother, deeply in love with the Child Jesus; she conferred with him often. She was also in contact with the Venerable Ludovico of Casoria, a reformed Franciscan of notable social initiatives († 1885); at his death Mother Rosa wrote: «How beautiful is the soul of Father of Casoria! Oh, how great he is in heaven!» (M 5.3, p. 81; 7, p. 4). The expansion of the Institute in America, with the mission of Bolivia, began with the invitation addressed by the superior of the Franciscans, Fr. Simpliciano of the Trinity, who turned to the foundress because, in his mind, the Daughters of St. Anne were also «daughters of St. Francis» (FIOCCHI, II, p. 15). The Capuchin missionaries entered Eritrea as chaplains of the Daughters of St. Anne, after many insistences by Mother Rosa; once the apostolic prefecture was founded, there was close collaboration with them.

For several years, as said above, Mother Rosa had as confessor the minister general of the Franciscans, Fr. Bernardino of Portogruaro. Finally, she was assisted in her last moments and received the holy Anointing from her last confessor, the Capuchin Fr. Vincenzo d'Alatri (FIOCCHI, II, p. 2938).

In 1873, when the ruptures caused by the suppressions of religious Orders in Catholic nations were still being felt and a climate of pessimism about their future was breathed, Mother Rosa foresees with superior light the glorious resurgence of the sons of St. Francis with the dawning of better days for the Church:

«I saw in the distance the peace of the Church and, moreover, the beautiful vocations that would arise in the Orders of St. Francis; so too among the religious women; but it was very distant…» (M 4.1, p. 16).

VI. UNDER THE IMPULSE OF APOSTOLIC CHARITY

The life of Rosa Gattorno is a demonstration of the Christian principle that true charity has two inseparable dimensions: one that has God as object and goal, the other that extends to all men, indeed to all beings. We already know in what way her spirit and her heart burned with this double impulse of love. Now we turn our attention to the apostolic dynamism, an essential requirement both of love for the Redeemer and of love for neighbor.

1. Zeal for the good of her spiritual daughters

Freed by God's will from family ties, but without extinguishing the flame of love for her own, Mother Rosa lived intensely for her new religious family, loving with a mother's heart each of the daughters of St. Anne, a love translated into solicitous interest, care, sharing of personal situations, longing for their spiritual progress and for their fidelity to the commitments assumed in profession.

Above all she wanted to see in the communities fraternal union, vivified by a generous, understanding and welcoming charity, to the point of «giving one's life» in service to others (cf. L to Sr. Francesca Camisa: 23-4-1867). In her letters to the superiors she expresses her joy when she hears that such a climate of union exists:

«You cannot believe how much consolation I felt on hearing how well you are all in agreement among yourselves. O blessed Charity! Well done, little daughter! May God pour upon your head his choicest blessings!» (L to Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi: 28-8-1880).

She suffers, on the contrary, when she observes divisions, murmurings, an atmosphere of suspicion and distrust. She rebukes one of the superiors because she does not put an end to the murmurings, which she herself favors by listening to accusations and impassioned reports (L to Sr. A. Sismondini: 9-4-1880). In the circular letter of 20 August 1893 we find harsh expressions regarding superiors who, instead of bearing lovingly with difficult sisters, write to the superior general: «Change her for me, change her for me!». Likewise against those who do not know how to keep secret the problems and defects of their fellow sisters and do not rather help them with gentleness to amend.

She lives with her heart always among the sisters. In a letter she recounts how, returning from Sicily, she met a holy religious, who, after looking at her attentively, said to her traveling companions: «The Mother, from Sicily returned half; the other half she left in Sicily». And she comments: «He truly told the truth: within myself I confirmed it. So, dear little daughters, with you I am and will be!» (L to Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi: 26-3-1885).

She has compassion and teaches compassion for afflicted fellow sisters, shares their difficulties with expressions of unspeakable tenderness, but without sentimentality. She writes to one of them:

«Your pains I carry with me and always make of them an offering to God, so that one day they may shine upon your head and with greater glory you may occupy that beautiful place that Jesus has prepared for you. Courage!» (L to Sr. A. Aquilina Gilardoni: 10-10-1889).

p. 1030

And to another:

«You cannot believe how much it grieves me to see you so afflicted. I do not want it! the tribulations that hurt us most are the sensible ones, but for this reason we must not dwell on them. No! a generous offering to God, and enough… Courage, dear little daughter, for I take lively part in your sorrow; but God so permits, so that we may detach ourselves from everything and ever more be for Him… Do not fear, for I am always with you!» (L to Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi: 13-7-1887).

In her letters her concern for the health of individual sisters becomes almost a topos. First of all for spiritual health: she experiences true trepidation at the mere thought that anyone might be unfaithful to the Lord. Writing to a superior in America about the case of a young professed sister who is in crisis, she orders her to do on her behalf whatever is necessary, transferring her wherever suitable, sparing no journeys: that vocation must be saved (L to Sr. A. Aquilina Gilardoni: 29-10-1898).

As regards care of bodily health she shows herself solicitous. She recommends not overdoing in apostolic work and in household chores. She wants to know the state of health of all, especially of those affected by some illness; of the gravely ill she wants news every day.

She, who all her life tormented her body with penances and fasts, lives concerned about the «excesses» the sisters can commit in the practices of penance. It is worth more before God — she teaches — to have health to be useful to the community and to the works of apostolate than to disable oneself with indiscreet privations and excessive labors. «First is your health, then the rest», she wrote to Sr. A. Pierina Della Valle (20-8-1895). Above all, never economize at the cost of the sisters' health, she recommends to the superiors (cf. L to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 9-5-1867; to Sr. A. Santina Solenghi: undated; to Sr. A. Aquilina Gilardoni: 17-10-1885). There is, however, no conflict between poverty and charity. In a circular of 1883 she makes this observation:

«In our visits we find that the economical superiors maintain the sisters, in food and clothing, even better than those who waste. So we recommend economy, both for love of poverty and for love of piety toward the Institute itself».

p. 1031

— In 1885 she wished to establish in Sicily a «fine infirmary», where the sisters of the region could be cared for, in order to spare the sick the hardships of transfers (L to Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi: 29-6-1885).

What she recommended to the superiors she practiced herself. «She visited the sick sisters even at night and when no one noticed» (Summ., p. 266). And when human remedies did not serve to relieve the ill, she had recourse to divine help, obtaining miraculous healing, as happened more than once. She knew, however, that illness too becomes a true gift of God, a privileged instrument of purification:

«Infirmities are sent by God and He is pleased to visit us through them. Better infirmity than wickedness. Infirmities draw us close to God, attract graces upon the houses…» (L to Sr. A. Aquilina Gilardoni: 24-8-1889) 47.

2. Industrious charity toward the needy

Purified by sorrow and humiliation, in her widowhood, Rosa discovered, so to speak, her own identity in her dedication to the poor sick, assisting them both in hospital and at home: in them she found the image of her Crucified, who already filled her heart. Having become foundress, she would have wished, with the zeal of the daughters of St. Anne, to meet every bodily and spiritual need, every social wound, causing to arise homes for the elderly, children's nurseries, crèches for infants, foundling homes, assistance to prisoners, conservatories for repentant women, popular schools… (cf. FIOCCHI, II, pp. 145-166, 271).

She called the Daughters of St. Anne «poor servants of the poor» (L to Emilia di Fitalia: 12-5-1893). Her preference was for the poor sick; in the various foundations the initial work of charity was almost always assistance to the sick at home; even in those whose purpose was the school, free assistance to the sick was not to be lacking. The cholera of 1867 was like the trial by fire for the nascent Institute, and the more general one of the years 1884-1887 constituted almost a public test: the daughters of St. Anne gave themselves heroi-

Casa Generalizia Figlie di S. Anna (Roma 1987). cally, especially in Naples and in Sicily; some died victims of the contagion (FIOCCHI, I, pp. 153-158, 179f; II, 69-89).

The foundress's legitimate pride in the heroism of her daughters is reflected in the circular letters of these years.

Those were also the times in which the work of mercy of giving food to the hungry had a quite concrete sense, in Europe too: the soup that was distributed in so many convents and shelters, especially in industrialized cities, where a defenseless proletariat, product of capitalist liberalism, struggled every day for subsistence. We read in the circular of 31 January 1880:

«God's mercy has called us, his ministers, to relieve so many wretched people, distributing to them every day food and clothing. In the Mother House alone, daily 3,000 beggars are fed with good and well-seasoned soup. What a grace this is, sisters! What a sign of predilection the Lord gives us!».

In all there were 4,522 bowls of soup that the Daughters of St. Anne distributed daily at three places in the city of Piacenza (L to Sr. A. Letizia Sordi: 15-1-1880).

Not only did she encourage the sisters to spend themselves in initiatives answering social realities, but she also stirred up the benefactors and friends of the Institute. In her letters to the princess of Fitalia she insistently spurs the charity of this spiritual daughter of hers to be generous toward «the wretched both of soul and of body». On 18 August 1892 she wrote to her asking her to help a poor mother with four children, abandoned by her husband. On 15 November 1896 she expressed to her her concern for so many poor in the coming winter, which was announced as severe. Again on 13 September 1897: «If you do not help me, this winter what will become of my poor?».

She knew, however, how to distinguish mere beneficence from authentic Christian charity, which gives with love and with humility, without protectionism or bureaucratic structures. She wrote in the circular of 20 January 1892:

«Be humble with the poor; always think that you are the last and the most wretched of all the creatures who render their service to the Church and have the good fortune to be part of it».

She could not bear a trace of harshness toward the sick. She wrote to a superior about some sisters who behaved badly toward them: «Tell those wretches that they are the dishonor of the house and of the whole Institute» 48.

Her spirituality of the sick and the poor derived from faith in the affirmation of Jesus: Whatever you did for one of these least of my brothers, you did for me (Mt 25:40) (cf. LCirc year 1876).

This faith had been at the beginning of her new life, in 1858, a true experience, like that which St. Francis of Assisi had when he kissed the leper, overcoming his repugnance, and then found sweet what before was bitter to him. Rosa kissed the ulcers of the sick and sometimes even passed her tongue over them (FIOCCHI, I, p. 43). Having found Jesus in the suffering, it was sweeter for her to contemplate the wounded Redeemer himself. One night, tired after a day wholly occupied in service to the sick, she had a rapture, in which she experienced the consolation of sucking the wound of the Lord's shoulder: having come to herself, she felt wholly invigorated (M 1.1, p. 59f). Another time, in 1864, after a similar experience contemplating the Lord's Passion, she wrote:

«My soul remained so strengthened that, returning to my work, I felt neither pain nor odor from my sick. It was sweet to serve them and in my God I felt I did everything» (M 2, p. 107).

In 1867, being in Rome, she went to the hospital. She wished to satisfy that avidity of hers to suck the wounds of the sick, but had to desist, both so as not to attract attention and so as not to be rapt in ecstasy by spiritual sweetness (M 1.1, p. 61).

She taught the same spirituality to the daughters of St. Anne, that is, how to motivate charity by seeing Christ in the needy and the suffering. She wrote in the same year to the sisters of the hospital of Cento:

«Console yourselves, you who toil for your Jesus. Ah! you always converse with Jesus, because in touching those sick with charity, you touch Jesus… In those sick creatures Jesus is found. Ah! what a thought, my daughters! I assure you that I feel I am dying of the desire to come to be with you, to take part in your

It is, however, interesting to note an evolution with the passing of the years, almost a purification of the motives of apostolic charity, an effect of a higher identification with the supreme Good. On 18 January 1875 Mother Rosa made the following profound introspection:

«Creatures, little by little become for me an object to cultivate and love, no longer as I still know I felt a sensible compassion for their ills, or of wanting them all holily, yes, but regarding them as if in the help and good I did them, or at least thought I did them, I found in them something of pleasure, which the charity done to them seemed to me must bring them.

Now I find nothing, nothing: purely my Good. Not even the smallest of created things do I know how to regard with a simple glance, if I do not first direct this too to Him…» (M 4.3, p. 185).

We find a similar reflection ten years later, on 17 July 1885 (M 5.3, p. 109f).

Among the works of mercy there is yet another: to teach the one who does not know. The apostolate of education in popular schools, at the service of the sons and daughters of the poor, appeared as a form of apostolic zeal already in the first years of the Institute, a service to society that with time will acquire notable importance. And in this sector of charity too Mother Rosa took care to give the daughters of St. Anne fully evangelical directives on how to treat the girls, with due respect for the person, always taking as model Mother St. Anne. But she was not slow to notice the danger that threatened the spirit of the Institute if the sisters assigned to teaching began to feel themselves of superior rank. In one of the circulars she expresses her concern at seeing that some of them seek to become «teachers»:

«Oh! if only this desire of yours came from a sublime sentiment of evangelization, of nourishing those hearts in the catechism and thus making them strong in our holy Religion! But unfortunately on this point there is something to deplore» (L Circ.: 20-1-1892). 3. Missionary universalism

The heart of Rosa Gattorno was a volcano in constant activity, insatiable of love. Here is an outpouring of hers in a letter to Sr. A. Celsa Speranza:

«I would like to attract the whole world, give to all, feed all. Oh! if only from my veins I could make gold come out for the poor! Do you know what I would do? By myself vein by vein I would want to draw it out until they were left dry. Oh! would I be satisfied? No! it is too ardent…» (L undated, no. 76).

One could compose a fine anthology with the effusions of her craving to make her dear Good known and loved, which leap out in the pages of her spiritual diary. Here are some:

«My Good, how can I make you known to the whole world? Oh! how many there are who do not know you! and those who have known you flee from you for never having seen you. I would like to run everywhere and cry out loud that all would come to love you» (Year 1862: M 1.1, p. 30).

«Oh! why do not all love you? Do you see, O my Good, the burning thirst I have to save souls?» (M 1.1, p. 33).

«O my Love! make use for once of this miserable instrument of yours to revive faith and the conversion of sinners!» — «All souls, come! Ah! love Jesus, do not offend Him!… I would have run through all the streets to cry out that they love Jesus. I threw myself face down on the ground and loudly asked the eternal Father to let me die a martyr to save the souls redeemed by Him. Am I not your instrument?» (Year 1867: M 1.1, pp. 60, 119).

«O my Love! how I feel myself burn with desire to make you known and loved by all! May your name be blessed by all tongues. My God! Oh! if only I could make all taste what I taste!» (M 1.2, p. 87).

Many of these outpourings are committed to paper after some of the most intimate experiences of the great mysteries that are communicated to her with infused light. She then thinks that so many others could share in such a good. On the feast of the Resurrection 1863, after a vision that filled her with consolation, she wrote: «O Love! why do you not let the unbelievers see a little of it?» (M 1.1, p. 1865). She often expresses her craving to go through the world to convert sinners, to suffer for them, to die a martyr for the salvation of the world, to see God loved by all.

p. 1036

At the moment of presenting the text of the Rules to the Pope, June 1871, while a shadow of harsh uncertainty weighed upon her soul, there emerged on the horizon of her faith a joyful future of missionary splendor:

«This horizon seems to me very dark for us, but the right hand of our eternal Father in an instant can dissipate everything and the Daughters of St. Anne Mother of the Immaculate enjoy the most beautiful light in all Catholicism and carry it to shine in the most idolatrous countries, and there plant the standard of St. Anne!» (L to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni: 2-6-1871).

She would like to make of every daughter of St. Anne a spokeswoman of Jesus to let all men hear the message of the Love that saves; that all might have the gift she experiences when she feels herself the pure instrument of Him who makes her speak. She wrote to her intimate Sr. A. Celsa Speranza:

«Jesus will put on your tongue words that you yourself will not know how you pronounced… love and think that it was Jesus who spoke in your heart and you were his echo, another» (L undated, no. 76).

What matters is, first of all, to evangelize with life (LCirc 20-8-1895). One of the sisters testifies in the informative process: «She wanted and imposed on us to act as missionaries in the hospitals, first by our bearing and then by charity and, finally, by word» (Summ., p. 458-459).

Two moments of deep joy the apostolic heart of Mother Rosa had: one, when she gave her maternal embrace to the sixteen sisters of the first expedition that left for Latin America on 23 November 1878, a harbinger of rapid expansion on that continent; and the other, that day when she presented to Leo XIII the four members of the first mission to East Africa, November 1886.

In her numerous letters to the missionary sisters one feels her heart throb as with a holy envy of the fortune they enjoy of being able to toil and suffer in the vanguards of the Kingdom of God. She would have wished to have so many daughters of St. Anne as to be able to satisfy all the requests that reached her. She wrote to the superior of Eritrea, Sr. A. Pierina Della Valle:

p. 1037

«My God, what pain not to have sisters!… Come, courage! I would like to be ten years younger and have strength; I would like to go and be a shoemaker! But I am very old and always very poorly» (L 8-11-1895).

From St. Francis of Assisi she had learned to see in the missionary vocation a free response to divine inspiration; the superiors of the houses in Italy were to keep her informed of the sisters who showed «vocation to go to the missions», but were to add «an exact and scrupulous report on their conduct», in order to guarantee the good choice of missionaries (LCirc: 25-3-1887, 23-4-1893).

VII. THE FOUNDRESS

The spiritual physiognomy of Rosa Gattorno would remain incomplete if her personality as foundress were left aside, indeed if the preceding chapters were not almost grafted onto her ecclesial mission and illuminated by her charism.

It does not, however, fall within the scope of this study to present the exceptional figure of the foundress of the Daughters of St. Anne in her historical reality, therefore tied to the origins and vicissitudes of this Institute, which would require a separate volume. I shall limit myself to highlighting, in synthetic form, those aspects in which certain evangelical traits are manifested in relation to the responsibilities assumed, by God's will, as guide of the Work. Moreover, several of these aspects have already been illustrated in the various themes developed, since it is not possible to detach her personal spirituality from her consciousness as foundress.

1. The weight of a mission beyond human measure

Rosa Gattorno found herself foundress at the end of an unplanned course, made under the impulse of charity, in submission to the hierarchical Church; indeed, one can say that it was obedience to the diocesan prelate and to the Roman Pontiff that placed her in the harsh alternative mentioned several times.

Like many other founders, she had the certainty that everything was the effect of a design traced from above. It was God, the eternal Father, who guided her steps along unknown paths, often disconcerting. No other is the interpretation she herself gave to the vicissitudes of God's Work, of which she considers herself a humble instrument, in her book Labors and Consolations: an anxious walking through dark woods and frightening precipices, a sailing on the stormy sea to bring the little boat to port; always fearful, but always sure of the assistance of her Crucified.

The more the experiential consciousness of her charism as foundress grows in her, the more she sinks into her own nothingness and unworthiness, and the more she fears being an obstacle to God's Work. She writes in February 1877:

«If I am benefited by someone, and praise is given to the Institute, and something is conferred on me, horror! I feel torn apart: such is my nothingness that rises before my eyes, that I remain as if humiliated, and I would throw myself on the ground, as I do when it is night, weeping. My God! an abyss of infamy is thought good and capable of doing good: it is impossible! Come! make known to all who I am, as you give me the grace to mirror myself in such deformed ugliness. Alas! never permit these poor creatures to remain betrayed by the exterior they see, but make them see what I see of miseries and infamy!» (M 4.4, p. 1185).

Deeply convinced, as she is, that everything is God's work, it comes naturally to her to attribute to Him every good outcome of the presence and action of the Daughters of St. Anne and the rapid expansion of the Institute; on the other hand, every time a difficulty arises or unpleasant news reaches her about the sisters' behavior, she attributes it to her own incapacity or her own faults:

«What shall I say? only that this happens because of me: behold my sins! Courage, let us trust in God: He, as it is his Work, will provide for everything» — «Ah yes, let me say it: this Work, the blows it takes are all fruit of my infamies. If so it pleases God, let us adore his divine Majesty» (L to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 6-8-1870, 16-11-1871).

This same consciousness of being herself the true obstacle to the course of God's Work made her think more than once of resigning and leaving to another the responsibility of general government. On noting, however, that such a thought assailed her precisely at moments of great grief on account of the Work, she suspected that it was suggested to her by the infernal enemy, and then she reacted as against a temptation, as if she wished selfishly to withdraw from the weight of her own mission. On 5 June 1880, on feeling herself accused by the bishop, unjustly, of helping her own sons with the Institute's goods, she wrote:

«I suffer immensely… I do not say what the enemy is suggesting to me; ah! he takes advantage, and so torments me immensely. He comes to tell me: "For you there will be no more peace"… Then I go on always studying how I can succeed in being put out of this office; I study it and almost this comforts me, when in my mind I find a means that seems to me to be the one that could help me to be removed and put in any lowly office. But I no longer pray for this. It is true that I see the traitor who at once seems to say: I have won!…» (M 4.5, pp. 196-205).

Mother Rosa's charismatic consciousness had a clarification and, I would say, a progressive growth. Without her realizing it herself, God made her mature through a series of liberations from the conditionings that successively prevented her from collaborating fully with the divine design, in the originality of her own evangelical line.

God led her to leave her Genoa to free her, not only from the proximity of her own family and relatives, but also from the social and religious commitments that bound her to the works and associations of which she had become the soul.

At Piacenza she felt freed and available for God's work. But here too she will have to untie herself from new conditionings that can divert the Institute's purpose or at least impede its spiritual and apostolic élan, shutting it in the narrowness of an asceticism without vigor or a paralyzing legalism.

She began by freeing herself from the direction of the priest Fr. Luigi Cogrossi, who had been the instrument of the choice of that city as cradle of the projected Institute. Rosa was not slow to notice that he was not the right man for the task of guiding the foundation, and she distanced him decisively.

Then came the providential meeting with Fr. Tornatore, priest of the Mission. Mother Rosa discovered in him the man whom the Lord sent her to guide her and be at her side in those beginnings; she entrusted herself to him without reserve and let herself be attracted by his personal piety, because the religious, besides being known for his doctrine as professor at the celebrated Alberoni College, was held by many in repute of holiness.

The foundress not only agreed to change the Institute's name, as has been said, following her own vision of Mother St. Anne, but would have wished Fr. Tornatore to be recognized as «first father» and founder, which, it seems, corresponded to his own intimate aspiration 49. In fact, she will always consider the Daughters of St. Anne as his daughters.

The liberation from Fr. Tornatore's influence was gradual, but complete. The first step was the separation between the internal and the external forum; Mother Rosa, as we have seen, very early interrupted spiritual direction with him and finally confession too. We think that a harmony between the spirituality of the co-founder and that of the foundress was not easy, already enriched with an intense infused experience and open to the great biblical and ecclesial horizons. But she wished to keep him at her side in everything that concerned the course of the Institute; indeed she had him designated by the diocesan bishop as ecclesiastical superior and asked the superior general of his congregation to leave him free of other commitments so that he could give himself fully to the Work (cf. FIOCCHI, I, pp. 222-241).

There was no lack of diversity of views, already in those beginnings, on the orientation to be given to the Institute. For example, when it was a matter of accepting the hospital of Cento, Fr. Luigi Cogrossi still having the direction, Fr. Tornatore gave a contrary opinion, because of the ambiguity he saw in that foundation, since Fr. Giambattista Tagiasco, who had asked for the sisters, wanted them not to appear as such, but as lay nurses 50. The foundress decided that foundation because it corresponded fully to her experience of this form of apostolic charity, but wanted the presence of the sister nurses as religious to be respected. It is interesting that, to make sure that such was God's will, Mother Rosa had re-

And Mgr. Scalabrini, in his reply to Cardinal Bilio, likewise designated him «founder» (cf. G.F. Rossi, Così la storia ricorda P. Tornatore, in Il ritorno del «Padre», Piacenza 1981, p. 4).

But the strong moment of liberation from dependence on the co-founder occurred in 1872, by drastic imposition of the Holy See. In the month of June she had delivered, together with him, the text of the Rules to Pope Pius IX. These had been drawn up by the religious in the form of a dialogue between St. Anne and her daughters, in a style and with a structure that the consultors found inadequate and gave a negative vote, indeed the text was transmitted to the Holy Office. After a long wait, the order arrived to burn all the copies, already printed, of the Rules and to remove Fr. Tornatore; he received the absolute prohibition to concern himself with the Daughters of St. Anne.

Certainly, there was no lack in the affair of the Rules of the intervention of persons opposed to Fr. Tornatore. However that may be, it was clear that, in Rome, they wanted to protect the Institute and the foundress herself from an orientation that was judged unsuitable.

Mother Rosa poured out, in the pages of her diary, the atrocious sufferings of that spring of 1872. She was convinced that the Rules had been written by the Father under God's inspiration; in them she had found formulated, substantially, the ideal and spirit of God's Work, according to the light she herself had received. In Vatican circles, however, she found nothing but prejudices and humiliating mockery, incomprehension. With no one to take counsel with, abandoned by God in darkness and aridity, she had moments in which she saw herself «led to the brink of despair» (M 3, p. 135).

She understood everything when she had the consolation of being received by Pius IX and heard from his lips: «I want this regulation to be extended by you alone». She herself tells it, and adds:

«Then he went on telling me to leave that priest, that is the T.; that it was better, because I would at last enjoy peace, I would no longer have to suffer so much… I thought: Who can have reported to him the pains he said I was suffering because of Mr. T.? It was true! But I had never told anyone what so fiercely I was going through» (M 2, pp. 68-71; 5, pp. 59-76).

Her humility and, in part, that mysterious bond that suffering itself had created between her and the co-founder, did not allow her to understand that as much distrust of the religious as there was in the Roman curia, just as much trust there was in her charism as foundress. The iter, nonetheless, was not easy. A first draft, made by her, was not accepted. She had to resign herself to leaving the work in the hands of some religious designated by the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars; but she reacted vigorously when she learned that they wanted to give the Daughters of St. Anne a legislation made along the lines of the constitutions of other institutes. On a new journey to Rome she defended the proper physiognomy of God's Work and obtained recognition of her right to intervene directly in the drafting. Thus they arrived at the approval ad experimentum, by decree of Card. Vannicelli, protector of the Institute, of 12 June 1874, of a text drawn up this time too by Fr. Tornatore.

The next protector, Card. Giuseppe Berardi, ordered Fr. Tornatore to write the Rules to present to the Congregation, since no one managed to make them and Mother Rosa had also rejected the text written by the consultor Fr. Bianchi. The new text was presented in January or February 1876 and in April the Institute obtained the decree of praise. The autograph manuscript of Fr. Tornatore exists at the Congregation of Religious. The text underwent successive modifications by the Congregation of Bishops and Religious and was definitively approved in 1892.

After some time, at the foundress's request, the co-founder was authorized by the Holy See to resume his office of ecclesiastical superior of the Institute and to intervene in its direction. In fact, the circulars that from time to time were addressed to the communities, although very often signed also by Mother Rosa, were written until 1888 by Fr. Tornatore.

The foundress, however, preferred to depend ever more immediately on the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars, through the Cardinal protector, above all after the pontifical approval of the Institute (21 April 1879). And it was the Cardinal prefect of the same Congregation who urged her to transfer the generalate seat to Rome to free her from the influences and conditionings of Piacenza, especially after what happened at the general chapter of 1881.

She felt herself ever more guided by God, free from the interference of anyone who did not live the Work from within. She wrote in the month of September 1887:

p. 1043

«O my Love! How well you maintain and direct your Institute!… It has no need of direction. Now I understand certain things that at times made me fear, but now that nothing is hidden from me any longer, tranquil I let everything go, thinking that by my Good all is ordered. Most holy Mary, my Mother! what a sweet thought it is to know that my Good Himself takes care to provide as is fitting the creatures for his Work! The labor that my poor head does is because he thus permits his slave to put in also the material effort to make with this the work complete» (M 5.5, p. 745).

Precisely at those dates Mother Rosa was enduring an ugly battle launched by Fr. Tornatore, by word and in writing, indeed harassing prelates and cardinals, in order to assert what he considered rights over the direction of the Institute. The letters of the years 1887 and 1888 to Mgr. Granito di Belmonte reflect the bitterness caused by the tiresome pursuit 51.

After the general chapter of 1888, during which he was ousted, the general government of the Institute did without Fr. Tornatore entirely. He, however, continued to love it as his work and to feel spiritually united to the Daughters of St. Anne. Even after his death, which occurred on 31 January 1895, one can say that he was officially ignored, until the Special Chapter of 1969-71 wished to rehabilitate him, recognizing him as Co-founder with full right. On 9 July 1981, in a rite presided over by the bishop of Piacenza Mgr. Enrico Manfredini, his mortal remains were translated to the Mother House 52.

Mother Rosa, who still on the occasion of the aforesaid chapter of 1888 and then in 1896 had «the temptation to renounce» (M 9.6, p. 12f), continued to feel herself a useless instrument of God's Work, directing it however with a sure hand together with her collaborators in the general government, having Mgr. Granito di Belmonte as external counselor and the Cardinal Protector as support in relations with the Apostolic See.

We already know of the foundress's maternal affection toward the spiritual daughters God gave her. Feeling herself responsible before Him who called them and entrusted them to her care communicates to her love a sense of presence among them, united to a lively pastoral consciousness that makes her all concern for their good.

The letters to the superiors and to individual sisters attest her delicate maternal attentions, almost meticulous, both regarding bodily health and the interests of the spirit. To express how she feels close to each she uses terms full of spontaneous cordiality:

«I keep you with me… everywhere I go» — «I feel all the sorrows you have and I told the Lord to transfer them onto my shoulders, for my breast already shares in the pain» — «I keep you near my right and every morning I commend you to God, my only All» — «You are nearer to me than if I had you at my side…» — «I always pray and can say in all truth that no morning passes that I leave church without praying in particular for all of you» 53.

She not only shares the anxieties and vicissitudes of the good religious, who console her heart, but also the situations and struggles of those who are in danger of infidelity to the commitments assumed; she prays for them, offers her penances for them. She writes on 19 September 1892:

«I had promised the discipline to blood if my Good granted me the conversion of a daughter of St. Anne who was in great danger of losing her vocation… I saw her free and returned wholly to Jesus» (M 12.2, p. 55).

With her feminine sense of detail, she keeps in mind all the particulars of every house. In a letter to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa, superior of the house of Piacenza, she asks her: «How are the flowers? The trees, have they taken? The doorkeeper's will be beautiful: tell her I was very satisfied with her labors and that the Holy Mother will keep her alive many years, let her not overwork» (IL 2-3-1872).

But the same pastoral solicitude entails vigilance, which knows how to forestall human weaknesses, and also timely correction.
