«I always noted her prudence in the reproofs she gave us, in which she was severe, yes, but had a something that compelled one to submit to her. When she then saw the sister repentant, she treated her gently and encouraged her» (Summ., p. 220).

She was less indulgent precisely with those she knew to be most attached to her, as appears in the letters to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa and Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni, both superiors. For the more important interventions she prepared herself with prayer and penances. In the month of August 1885, during the sisters' spiritual exercises, she observed that the sermons produced no fruit in them, because «they had their hearts soaked in worldly things». She prayed and did the discipline. Finally, on the day of the Assumption she felt impelled to intervene:

«Behold, this evening this ass was able to speak, and yes, they already came to manifest to me frankly that they learned nothing from the holy exercises, but that at the last word I told them, oh! all thrown at my feet they ask forgiveness and want to change. God has used mercy on them, what goodness!» (M 5.4, p. 625).

It was above all in the visits to the communities, in personal dialogue with individual sisters, that she knew how to join reproofs to maternal attentions. When one reads the notes she made rapidly, with truncated phrases, a rather negative impression remains of the spiritual and even moral level of the sisters. She discovers not only common defects, but notable abuses, hidden intentions, concealments and pretenses on the part of the superiors… She often exclaims as her sole comment: Horror! (cf. M fasc. 6, 7 and 8). Perhaps this pessimistic stance of hers is to be attributed to her innate introspection into the interior of persons as well as to her tendency to see black, acknowledged by her herself, as said elsewhere.

In the annual circulars to the whole Institute there are not lacking, alongside motives of encouragement for the growing vitality and development of God's Work, the negative observations and the laments of her sorrowing heart on account of non-observances and other «black points» that sadden Mother St. Anne.

As much as she loved to have information directly from the sisters themselves, so much did she abhor accusations and gossip that could harm someone's reputation or disturb the peace of the community (L to Mgr. Granito di Belmonte: 30-7-1896).

The personal visit to the houses and the meeting with the superiors and with each sister was, for Mother Rosa, the primary duty of her service as superior general. To bring her daughters the comfort of her presence, she faced the hardships of long journeys and the troubles of her illnesses. Her secretary Sr. A. Celsa Speranza testified in the Process:

«From the beginnings of the Institute's foundation I learned from other sisters that she visited the houses very often, and was always here and there, so much so that once, asked what her domicile was, she replied jokingly: On the railways! For the visit of the houses she did not shun hardships and sacrifices» (Summ., p. 245).

But there was also that other meeting, no less important, by means of an incessant correspondence, which occupied her whole days, to the point of giving the impression, not corresponding to the truth, of exercising a central government from a desk. The night for God in unitive contemplation, the day also for God, but occupied in her Work. There was no room for idleness. «Sin of idleness I have none — she wrote to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa —, the only one perhaps that I shall not find at God's tribunal, when all the others I have committed all of them» (L 15-10-1871).

On returning from journeys she found mountains of letters, to all of which she felt obliged to give a reply, which was not possible without the help of her secretaries. But the sisters were accustomed to those letters written in her own hand; through the strokes of her handwriting and her incisive phrases, it seemed to them they felt the beating of her mother's heart. Sometimes they complained of those impersonal letters, written by her order (cf. L to Sr. A. Gaudenzia Martinelli: 15-6-1880).

She experiences a special divine assistance in the heavy work, above all when to fatigue are added spiritual aridity and other sufferings.

«Dear Monsignor: The tribulations are daily, they never stop, never! one more terrible than the other. I feel shattered and I see my poor physique too worn down: the years, the continual journeys, the sufferings and more the terrible torment of my poor spirit tossed from all sides. I do not know how or where to calm myself. Work! I feel an obligation of conscience that drives me; humanity shrinks from work, it seems to have lost my energy…» — «After a long suffering I resolved to depart and begin my old life: it is better to die working than to give oneself over to cures!» (L to Mgr. Granito di Belmonte: 18-6-1888, 2-9-1893).

The same indomitable will to die under the weight of the mission of foundress she expresses in a fine paragraph of the circular of 7-12-1895:

«If nothing has been able until now to halt my step for your good and for the greater glory of God, I assure you that, to the last breath of my life, I shall always be the same and shall not fail to come to your aid in any need of yours».

In Mother Rosa's Memoirs there is frequent experiential observation of divine help through that charismatic gift of her own intuition about the situation of persons and about the signs through which God lets her know what is happening in this or that community, what is troubling this or that sister. Almost always these are painful situations that make her suffer and set herself to pray, redoubling her penances. Very often she feels that a higher light suggests to her what she must resolve in certain difficult cases concerning the Work (cf. M 4.2, pp. 81-84). She writes on 23 February 1875:

«When I must speak of certain little small things, it seems to me that I find them all easily in my mind, others grave ones of the Work yes cleared up in my mind, all as if I had to draw them out already prepared. Oh! how I think that I had not the slightest thought in this Work and only had the materiality of putting in its place what my Good goes on teaching me!» (M 4.3, p. 28).

3. The art of sharing the responsibility of government

It has often been observed that charismatic superiors are wont to be accused of authoritarianism, certainly not from ambition for power, but from the habit of feeling themselves enlightened and guided by God, with the danger of not valuing the opinions and proposals of others. There was no lack, within and outside the Institute, of persons who disagreed with that way of centralizing everything in her own person, attributed to the foundress. One of the most delicate moments in relations with the Holy See came when the order to constitute the general council was not obeyed, as moreover existed in all institutes of pontifical right. Mother Rosa asked pardon and obeyed humbly. There was, however, a motive of evangelical charity that led her not to keep even her own collaborators informed of matters concerning individual sisters: the right of these to the secrecy that a superior must observe about what she has learned by virtue of her office. In 1880 she left written an interesting reaction of hers:

«I had a sweet reproach from the Lord, who told me why I had left off a little always keeping silent about everything, even the smallest things of the Work, that I never said anything and that this was very pleasing to the Lord, whereas I had to do myself great violence to say something (I mean things of the Work, not things of me, no, oh! those never!).

But since I was charged by the Protector with being too secretive and that it was not right, that in this way the poor sisters would never learn anything, but that I was obliged to say what was going on to those who were near me in order to instruct them more and tell them how I acted to remove that abuse or imperfection or other thing that was happening: so, although I did it with repugnance, I did it nonetheless, I can say by force of obedience.

Oh! when I heard this reproach, it was most dear to me, because it takes nothing to put it into practice. So I can say I have closed, and it is finished. Yes, my Good, I shall speak no more. And to tell the truth, besides having the repugnance, I saw still that I obtained no good from it, quite the contrary, indeed I brought back ill humors. I always in the past had abstained, and so all men and women thought well of the daughters of St. Anne, although one and more than one attacked me. Oh! my silence too did good, it brought no displeasure (?), no one knew anything, everything remained in me» (M 4.5, pp. 187-189).

Mother Rosa was convinced that the good course of the Institute depends, first of all, on the wise choice of superiors and their responsible care for the good of the sisters. Certainly, the rapid growth of the Work with the multiplication of houses in Italy, in America and in Africa made it difficult to find suitable superiors for every community. From the correspondence with them and, above all, from the circulars, often very harsh, one deduces that not all were equal to the task entrusted to them. The foundress feels it her duty to denounce with raw sincerity the unevangelical behavior of the superiors, but also to form them and guide them in the right way of governing. Besides the correspondence kept with each, she makes use of the aforesaid circulars and, in a special way, of the conferences on the occasion of visits, gathering them by zones, and of the general chapters, which are usually preceded by a course of spiritual exercises.

She has an ideal image of the superior, whose traits she seeks to inculcate at every opportunity. First of all, she bitterly stigmatizes the ambition to become superior, «accursed vice that reigns in the Institute», as well as «pride, vanity, vainglory» that dominates in many, as she was able to verify in the visits; she prays the Lord to give back to her «daughters full of his love, humble, ready to receive any office, from superior at Javandaia to superior in the kitchen» (LCirc: 15-6-1894).

The first task of a superior is to be guide and support of her sisters in fidelity to their vocation, knowing that «they will have to render account to God for their souls» (LCirc: 1890, 20-1-1892). But she cannot be an effective guide if she herself is not for them a model and example:

«Superiors are the shadow of the other religious, who all run after them and go as the shadow shows them the way» (L to Sr. Francesca Camisa: 13-5-1872) — «The superior must be the lighthouse that guides all to the safe harbor… Care for the interests of your heavenly Spouse, win souls for him. Courage then and holy rivalry with your beloved sisters in the advancement of the virtues!» (L to Sr. A. Gerarda Canovi: 30-4-1900) — «Superiors are the candelabras from which, as their torch burns, the others entrusted to them light one another, and true torches burning with sacrifice and love, they seek to be consumed in the burning Heart of Jesus» (LCirc.: 3-3-1897).

The superior must be the first in the observance of the Rules and in punctuality at the common acts. Her presence in the chores and her participation in fraternal recreation also contributes to the good atmosphere of the community. She wrote to one of them in these terms:

«One does not go to recreation thinking it is something made for those scatterbrained ones, but not for them; and so stupid singularities are made. Go to recreation, humble yourselves, proud ones, speak with your sisters…» (L to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni: 25-8-1869).

p. 1050

The virtues she most desires to see in superiors are: «charity, prudence, humility and patience» (L to Sr. A. Del Tabor Saldini: 28-4-1900; to Sr. A. Agnese Facchini: 29-4-1900). She insists in a special way on gentleness, avoiding all harshness in corrections. Indeed the art of knowing how to correct at the opportune time and manner, without becoming upset, without humiliating, with the sole aim of doing good to the guilty or simply negligent sister, is not easy. Mother Rosa, in her letters, gives serious warnings to superiors who show themselves harsh or let themselves be dominated by the first impulse in corrections and adds advice of great wisdom on how to exercise this pastoral duty (cf. L to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni: 1871 [or 1869]; to Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi: 10-7-1885, 29-12-1885).

If it is true that the foundress had reasons for personally carrying out throughout her life, assisted by her most faithful secretaries, the general government of the Institute, it is equally true that she respected on principle the responsibility of the local and regional superiors, giving them the greatest trust in the decisions and initiatives to be taken. Indeed, she encourages them to act with mature personal choices, after having consulted. She wrote to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa, too accustomed to turning to her dear Mother for everything:

«My dear daughter, try to become more self-assured…; in certain cases you must govern yourself: first commend yourself to God, and then, forward, with courage!» (L 27-8-1872).

In letters to other superiors we find similar words of trust in what they will decide for themselves:

«You have done everything well, I approve all you do, go ahead with courage!» «When I receive your letters and see that you act as God inspires you, they bring me immense consolation. Courage!» — «I would not know what to tell you: commend yourself to St. Anne and then do what you feel inspired to do» — «I want you to take the matter as advice and not as a command: you are closer and are well placed to see things in a better light» — «I leave you in full freedom to do what you think best» — «All that you have done is very good, and indeed take care always to do so, because you know the needs of the house» — «What do you say? I await from you whether you approve» — «Cheer up! and so the sisters too. Do not worry, for Jesus is there thinking for you: you think for Him, for He thinks for you» — «You have done excellently…, do not worry; I approve what you have done and what you will do» — «I leave everything to your wisdom and I will always approve all that you do, knowing how the good of the Institute is dear to you» — «I know that you do better than all the suggestions, courage!» — «Of everything I tell you that you do well and I am content».

What prevented the sisters from acting with freedom of spirit in their responsibilities was, besides the little trust some had in themselves, the fear of not cutting a good figure in the eyes of the foundress, who was known to be abreast of what happened in every house. Precisely this assiduous information kept certain superiors uneasy, who tried to hinder the free communication of their subjects with the superior general; she denounces several times, in the circulars, such a violation of right, which obeys the «fear that the sisters may write to the Mother about them: this fear is born of duplicity» (LCirc: 31-1-1880).

«You harm yourselves both with regard to us and with regard to your subjects, because to us you give cause to suspect that you do things contrary to your duty, and to your subjects the reason to think that you are not in harmony with us. How different is that community where the subjects and the superior are well harmonized with us! I can assure you that the superior is loved and respected; the thoughts in that community agree; there is no murmuring, there are no subterfuges, and the peace of the Lord makes them overcome every sacrifice» (LCirc.: 2-3-1895).

From experience, however, of the content of many letters that reached her by that route, she was not unaware that very often they were inspired by resentments or personal interests; in them one perceived «a perfect sound of murmuring» (L to Mgr. Granito di Belmonte: 13-8-1890).

Although her first concern was to form the superiors in the art of governing well, since as a rule when one governs well one obeys well, she did not fail to inculcate in all the daughters of St. Anne the life of obedience, which «is the pivot of true holiness» (LCirc: 1-1-1889). «Obey if you want to be saints», she repeated in the communities (L to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 4-5-1869). «On the way to paradise it is written: Obedience» (M 4.4, p. 14).

She taught the sisters to «see in their superiors the person of dear Jesus, and not to be demanding in wanting the superior to be perfect in everything» (LCirc: 1890). 4. Formation: criteria and methods

The overly accelerated growth of a nascent institute risks launching into space a leafy tree lacking deep roots. Mother Rosa had to hear more than once from respectable persons such an appraisal of the Daughters of St. Anne, as appears in her book:

«One of the pastors said to me in an altered tone:

— I tell you that your way of proceeding is poorly founded… In the work you do you run too much: a brake is needed, otherwise these workers will do nothing good…

Ironically he went on to say:

— Know that I liken these fields to the pumpkin plant, which runs and is all leaves; in the end its fruit is a pumpkin!

Then I answered him:

— The time will come when this pumpkin will harden and give you indigestion! It will rise above all the plants and, finally, will stretch its branches from one pole to the other, its roots will not be able to suffer any molestation…, its fruits will be tasty to the Spouse of my Lord and the flowers will have an odor all their own…» (TC, p. 2745).

She understood from the beginning that the means of making «the pumpkin harden» was the solid formation of the Daughters of St. Anne. Aware of so serious a responsibility, she trembled at the thought that she would have to render account to God for so many souls entrusted to her direction: «How shall I get out of it before God's tribunal?» (M 3, p. 71). She was particularly gifted to be a spiritual guide and possessed an ascendancy over the sisters that guaranteed the favorable reception of her teachings and demands. What she lacked in human culture and pedagogical preparation, her intuition, guided by light from above, and her experience abundantly supplied. To judge from the letters, a good number of sisters, above all of the first generation formed personally by her at Piacenza, continued to receive from their Mother true spiritual direction, in which affectionate encouragements alternated with the harshest reproofs.

But she was not content with this personal guidance. She was solicitous in common instructions; «every Sunday she convened all the religious of the community to exhort them about their religious duties» (Summ., p. 46). «Besides the conferences that Mr. Tornatore often gave, besides the exercises that she had them given, she often invited some religious to give sermons» (Summ., p. 196). Mention was made above of the conferences, even true courses of formative conferences, diligently prepared by her, of which numerous outlines and also verbatim transcriptions made by the secretaries are preserved; many of them concern quite concrete particulars of the behavior of a daughter of St. Anne both in community life and outside the house.

She gave much importance to the influence, positive or negative, that confessors and spiritual directors could exert on the formation of the sisters. She complains of certain directors too ready to believe in the extraordinary graces that some sisters say they have received from God, making them write, etc.; the result is that «they exalt themselves in imagination» (M 5.3, p. 308; 5.4, p. 23; 5.5, pp. 15-19; 9.1, pp. 18-20). The worst was when they tried to make them lose trust in the foundress:

«Certain pastors were so little capable of giving a true and sound direction to those dear workers, that they gave me much pain. Moreover they believed they could succeed in putting me out of the field in order to overturn once more that beautiful cultivation» (TC, p. 2705).

In the circulars superiors are reminded of the obligation to procure suitable priests for the conferences to the community, above all for the annual holy exercises. She was demanding in the choice of such ministers of the Word, especially when it could be harmful to the spirit of the Institute. In 1892 she asked Mgr. Granito di Belmonte for «a good and holy priest» to give the spiritual exercises to the sisters; but, fearing that the one designated was a renowned priest, she excluded him: «I would not want it to be he: no, no! He does not know our spirit, he is not at all for the Daughters of St. Anne. He may be a saint, but of another spirit and not ours. Are we agreed?» (L 18-8-1892).

To the superiors she not only inculcated the means of spiritual and moral formation, but also those suited to intellectual and technical instruction. She wanted every community to have a small library, stocked above all with books of spirituality (cf. L to Sr. A. Ancilla Briccoli: 11-4-1895).

But the most solicitous care was for the formation of the young candidates. The witnesses of the informative process note the seriousness with which the foundress proceeded in the admission of postulants, excluding without regard those she saw were not suitable (Summ., pp. 13, 373, 456). She gave no importance, however, to the possibility of bringing a dowry, if the candidate showed a good vocation. Those who, during postulancy, behaved in a way that left doubts about the sincerity of their vocation, she ordered to be dismissed as soon as possible (cf. L to Sr. A. Paola Bucciotti: 20-5-1872; to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 5-9-1872; to Sr. A. Francesca Savignoni: 13-3-1880; to Sr. A. Gaudenzia Martinelli: 6-4-1885).

The novitiate, time of more intense formation and of experience of consecrated life, was a special object of her care. Not content to entrust the novices to a suitable mistress, she took care of them personally by means of her conferences. Twenty-three of these instructions are preserved and several outlines of others, given to the novices on various dates. In general they contain a first part of an ascetical nature and then what she calls «religious galateo», that is, practical advice on social and religious courtesy, personal hygiene, self-mastery, etc.; all suggested by the commentary on the Rules (M 10.2, 10.3).

At the beginning of the foundation the young women, after six months of novitiate, were sent to houses where there were urgent needs, especially in case of epidemic (Summ., p. 374). Later she preferred that they begin the novitiate after having tried them «in the work of holy charity in assisting the sick» (M 5.5, p. 65).

Formation did not end with the novitiate nor with the time of temporary vows. What we might call «ongoing formation» was entrusted to the individual superiors and, at the level of the Institute, provided by the foundress herself, for some years with the collaboration of Fr. Tornatore, by means of circular letters, as said above. The goal toward which such formation tended was the holiness of each of the daughters of St. Anne. «May the Lord make you saints and great saints», she repeats in the letters. She wrote to Sr. A. Celsa Speranza:

«Tell me, do you believe that I want one thing only: your sanctification? Yes, it is true. Well, I, a great wretch that I am, do not cease to ask my God that, through the merits of my dear Crucified, he sanctify you all. In clasping myself to Him when I am in my poor room, oh! with what strength I clasp you in his Heart! O sweet Love! Yes, my dear daughter, seek me in Him and I promise you that you will always find me» (L undated, no. 76).

In the Memoirs we find supplications like this: «All of them I would wish to be according to your Heart, my Love!» (M 11.2, p. 825). And in a circular of 1893: «We nourish a great desire to be able to see you all according to the heart of God» (LCirc: 23-4-1893). And, as a sure means to walk according to God's will and attain holiness in the life embraced, she insists on the observance of the Rules, «the pivot that holds the wheel firm and makes it run with exactness» (LCirc: 20-2-1893).

5. The «Sons of St. Anne»: an idealistic project that did not succeed

Mother Rosa speaks of the foundation of the Sons of St. Anne as early as 1882: a male institute to stand beside the Daughters of St. Anne, to form with these and with the tertiaries of St. Anne, already mentioned 54, the three Orders, symbolized in the three drops of blood that had been shown to her in a vision. In September of the same year she had been encouraged by «a learned and holy Franciscan» to begin that foundation in earnest (M 5.1, pp. 89-94; 5.2, pp. 625, 66f, 1055).

And it was precisely her desire to provide suitably and in a stable form for the formation of the Daughters of St. Anne according to the spirit of the Institute that urged her to such a work.

«How I see the need of having the Sons of St. Anne! What pains it is to see these poor creatures guided by different spirits, because one tends to withdrawal, the other too lax lets go the bridle and they find themselves dissipated. And that inner voice:

— Put your hand to the work: they will help you!…

But I feel an enormous repugnance, so that I do not know how even to think of it; it is so strong that it overcomes me. My Love, I shall await obedience and to this I shall submit everything» (M 5.1, pp. 295, 58, 60; 5.5, p. 5).

54 It is not clear what the «third order» was in Mother Rosa's mind: the «tertiaries of St. Anne», who will begin at Piacenza in 1884, as said above, or a third order of laity, of which she had spoken with the princess of Fitalia, according to her deposition in the process?

The project took shape in 1886: Fr. Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, received in private audience by Pope Leo XIII on 6 December 1886, set out his intentions orally. The Pontiff invited him to summarize his ideas in writing, which he did on 8 December, entrusting the paper to Mgr. Marzolini, a person very close to the Pope; not receiving a direct reply he urged the same Monsignor and the Pontiff, by the same route, made known to him his will: he should begin the work at Naples under the direction of the Archbishop, then to proceed, with the latter's letter of recommendation, to ask for pontifical approval. Fr. Gennaro then asked Card. Sanfelice to begin the work (L 6-1-1887) setting out the steps already taken. A few days later, on 10 January, the Cardinal replied: not expedient.

The project of the «Sons of St. Anne» having failed, the following year, 1888, Fr. Gennaro thought of doing something pleasing to Mother Rosa and useful to himself and to other priests, to gather those priests who already rendered their ministry in the sisters' houses, forming a Devout League of priests for the good of the Daughters of St. Anne. Without consulting Mother Rosa further as to the form (L 16-5-1888, end of May 1888; M 9.4, p. 13f), he laid the project before the Archbishop of Naples on 26 August and Card. Sanfelice approved the work on 28 August. Fr. Gennaro informed Mother Rosa (the letter, unfortunately, has been lost) and the Foundress, fearing that these priests would go, without other formation or preparation, to the sisters' houses to preach spiritual exercises, gave her flat no to such an idea (L 31-8-1888). Then she wrote in her diary:

«The begun work of the Sons of St. Anne gives me great pain, because I see it is not as God desires it. It seems to me rather a wanting to undertake too much the direction of the Daughters of St. Anne without first being well identified with the Work and seeking to have its true spirit, more than not knowing what our Constitutions and customs are; moreover they think too soon they are good at directing. After 22 years of continual struggles and of studying the character of the sisters and the position they are in!…

Oh! if I were good at explaining the wound I received when it was announced to me! Oh! what I felt on hearing that, without any agreement everything is done and ordered as if they were our superiors! What pain I felt on hearing that these would go to preach in the houses! My God! what will happen? All this without knowing anything. I see and feel that Jesus does not find his pleasure…» (M 9.5, pp. 87-91).

p. 1057

Fr. Gennaro, faced with Mother Rosa's lively reaction, defended himself in a letter to Card. Alimonda (5-9-1888) explaining that these priests would be only «most humble servants of the Daughters of St. Anne» and would have «no interference or jurisdiction over the sisters». The Devout League, in any case, had no sequel.

Thus the project of a male branch went up in smoke. Mother Rosa resigned herself to the failure, convinced that, conceived in that way, as a pure external, paternalistic help, that foundation was of no interest, indeed would have been harmful to the Daughters of St. Anne.

CONCLUSION

At the end of my work, after having classified and interwoven hundreds of data drawn above all from the Memoirs and the letters of Mother Rosa, I still find myself with a heap of unused index cards, even if they contain information and ideas that could enrich some of the aspects already set out of the physiognomy of the Servant of God as well as offer material for other chapters on the various evangelical virtues, such as for example poverty, humility, chastity, temperance… But in a synthesis like this one entrusted to me it is not the case to exhaust the investigation — consider the more than nine thousand letters — nor to complete every detail. Whoever then wishes to know the way in which Mother Rosa exercised each of the virtues to a heroic degree may have recourse to the Positio super virtutibus that will be printed by the Congregation for the Causes of Saints.

I hope that the seven chapters, worked out by me with care and affection, will be sufficient to outline in all its dimension the genuinely Christian, truly exceptional personality of Rosa Gattorno and to propose to the Daughters of St. Anne the great model of experience of God and of active charity that they have in their spiritual Mother.
